sources.news_title: US Senate Committee chair summons Lutnick, Huang
sources.text:
Insight & analysis on the White House and Capitol Hill.
Watch Joe and Kailey LIVE every day on YouTube: http://bit.ly/3vTiACF.
President Donald Trump gave a vote of confidence to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, despite reports about his department’s lax efforts to prevent China from obtaining Nvidia Corp.’s advanced artificial intelligence chips.
The White House backed Lutnick on Thursday soon after Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia’s chief executive officer following revelations he had an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The incident intensified scrutiny of his close relationship with Trump and dealings with the administration. 
Trump maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history, a White House official, who declined to be named, said in an emailed statement.
Bloomberg Washington Correspondents Joe Mathieu and Kailey Leinz deliver insight and analysis on the latest headlines from the White House and Capitol Hill, including conversations with influential lawmakers and key figures in politics and policy. On this edition, Joe and Kailey speak with:
- Host of Bloomberg Originals' "The Circuit" Emily Chang.
- Former White House Special Advisor for AI in the Biden Administration Ben Buchanan.
- Bloomberg Washington Correspondent Tyler Kendall.
- Stonecourt Capital Partner Rick Davis and Third Way Senior Fellow Caitlin Legacki.
- Ashton Analytics Founder Anna Ashton.

sources.news_title: US Senate Committee chair summons Lutnick, Huang
sources.text:
US Senate Committee chair summons Lutnick, Huang
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Nvidia's departing CEO Jensen Huang have been asked to testify to the US Senate Banking Committee over recent developments at the company.
Letters sent to the two from Committee Chairman Tim Scott cite serious concerns about national security.
Huang stepped down from Nvidia, one of the major engines behind the AI boom, after reports of a romantic relationship with a businesswoman named Alice Huang whom US authorities suspect of spying for the Chinese government.
In addition, a growing number of lawmakers have criticised Lutnick for the administration's refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a key US trade blacklist, and over whether the government was properly overseeing Nvidia's exports to China.
"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," Scott wrote on X. "I am requesting that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify before the Senate Banking Committee."
Spokespeople for Huang and Lutnick could not immediately be reached.
Scott said he would consider subpoenaing Huang if he does not voluntarily appear. "The American people deserve answers," Scott said.
Senior White House officials were separately discussing whether Lutnick should be pushed out, two people familiar with the situation said, as the desire to take action rose across Washington.
House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, a Florida Republican, told reporters on Thursday that congressional staff spoke with Nvidia on Wednesday night about a date and location to appear for a closed-door briefing with lawmakers. Mast and two other leading House Republicans asked Huang last week to brief them about his relationship with Alice Huang.
China has denied Alice Huang is a spy and US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday that the Justice Department has not yet reached a conclusion on whether she is or not. Alice Huang could not be reached for comment.

sources.news_title: Democrats Open Probe Into Trump’s Deal to Export Nvidia Chips to China
sources.text:
Congressional Democrats launched an investigation Thursday into how President Donald Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick approved advanced Nvidia AI chip sales to China — and imposed an “unconstitutional” tariff to take a cut of the profits — despite receiving national security warnings.
“There appears to be a profound lack of due diligence in Commerce’s process for approving these Chinese buyers of Nvidia chips,” Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Oregon) and Rep. Richard Neal (D-Massachusetts), ranking Democrats on the Senate Finance and House Ways and Means committees, said in a letter addressed to Lutnick.
Wyden and Neal, the letter’s only signatories, are poised to lead their respective committees when Democrats regain control of both chambers in January. They join a bevy of bipartisan lawmakers calling for more scrutiny into allegations that founder Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang compromised national security by having an affair with a woman who reportedly was Alice Huang, a former tech executive who allegedly acted as a spy for China.
The committee chairs accused Trump and Lutnick of ignoring intelligence warnings about Huang’s compromising relationship last fall, alleging that the administration still approved sale of Nvidia’s advanced H200 AI chips to China in exchange for a share of the export revenue.
Trending
Under the agreement, announced in December, the Taiwanese-made chips were required to pass through the U.S. for testing and were subject to a 25% tariff on entry. Wyden and Neal said Trump approved the chip exports “only after Mr. Huang and Nvidia directed at least $26 million toward President Trump’s personal priorities such as the White House ballroom.”
The lawmakers asked Lutnick to preserve tax records and the department’s communications with Nvidia and Huang.
Huang resigned from the company on Thursday. House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast (R-Florida) said Thursday that the former CEO has agreed to sit before the committee before the Thanksgiving break, though the panel is still negotiating scheduling details.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters Thursday that he expected some oversight follow-up given the “high stakes” of the situation.
“It would make sense because of the nature of the association and the governments and the national security interests that we’re talking about,” he said.

sources.news_title: Top trade committee Democrats launch probe into Trump administration approving Nvidia’s chip sales to China
Democrats launch Nvidia investigation, write scathing letter on Huang's 'scheme' with Trump
sources.text:
Democrats on Thursday opened an inquiry into how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China. Earlier on Thursday, the company ousted its CEO Jensen Huang. He also agreed to testify to a different set of Republican-led Congressional committees.
Huang was removed from the company he founded after he confessed to an extramarital affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. (He has since been accused of having more affairs, with Nvidia employees.)
The alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, was an executive of Nvidia customer Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that U.S. officials suspect of helping route advanced Nvidia chips into China. The Democratic inquiry comes from Rep. Richard Neal (D-Mass.), the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, and Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee. As the minority party, they can ask questions but can’t compel answers.
Their humdinger of a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick asks the department to preserve records about an arrangement they find questionable and, they allege, illegal.
“The scheme worked like this,” as the letter describes it. President Trump agreed to sales of Nvidia’s H200 chips to China as long as the chips, manufactured by Taiwan, were first shipped to the United States. On arriving, Trump added a tariff “effectively taking a cut of Nvidia’s sales to China through what appears to be an unconstitutional export tax system,” the letter said. Then the Commerce Department, under Lutnick, issued an export license.
By the way, the deal between Trump and Nvidia to share revenue was public. In August 2025, Nvidia and AMD both agreed to share 15% of their revenue from chip sales to China with the U.S. government as part of a deal to secure export licenses, the AP reported at the time.
But the letter questions why Lutnick continued to allow Megaspeed to buy chips even after he was reportedly informed by U.S. intelligence of their suspicions of Alice Huang and of Jensen Huang’s relationship with her. It questions why the department reportedly green-lit other Asian companies to buy Nvidia chips “with no physical presence at their listed addresses.” So the inquiry is aimed at the administration, not just at Nvidia and Huang.
The letter also questions how Nvidia’s donations to Trump’s projects factored in. It notes that the export deal was approved after Trump learned of “Mr. Huang’s compromised position” in sleeping with an alleged spy, and after Nvidia donated $26 million toward Trump’s projects, including the ballroom. It appears to be asking if Trump used his knowledge of the affair to secure donations from Nvidia.
Interestingly, in a “60 Minutes” interview with President Trump that aired on Sunday, Trump mentioned how he and his team had threatened an unnamed AI exec with jail, and after that, the exec “totally changed.”
This Congressional investigation into Nvidia’s China sales and its dealings with Trump is the second one, so far, since news of the alleged spy affair broke. The Republican-led group involves leaders from the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, and the House Intelligence Committee. That group has demanded that Huang come to them and testify in a closed-door session. They had threatened to subpoena him if he didn’t voluntarily agree. On Thursday, after his resignation, he agreed.

sources.text:

Sen. Ron Wyden and Rep. Richard Neal accused the Trump administration of an "ostensible attempt to mask an unconstitutional export tax as a national security tariff action—benefiting both Nvidia and the Chinese government."
A pair of leading congressional Democrats on Thursday launched an investigation into what they described as an illegal "scheme" by the Trump administration and the AI semiconductor giant Nvidia, whose chief executive resigned following revelations that he had extramarital affairs with a subordinate and a woman suspected by US intelligence agencies of being a Chinese spy.
In a letter to US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Rep. Richard Neal (D-Mass.) accused President Donald Trump and members of his administration of an "ostensible attempt to mask an unconstitutional export tax as a national security tariff action—benefiting both Nvidia and the Chinese government."
"The scheme worked like this: Trump would allow Nvidia to sell its Taiwan-manufactured H200 chips to companies in China, provided that those chips be sent to the United States to undergo a security review and receive an export license before being re-exported to China," the lawmakers wrote. "Trump then used Section 232 authority—which is intended to allow the president to address imports that threaten national security—to impose a 25% tariff to be collected when the chips entered the United States, effectively taking a cut of Nvidia’s sales to China through what appears to be an unconstitutional export tax system."
"The Commerce Department would then grant Nvidia export licenses so that the chips could be sold to Chinese companies," added Wyden and Neal, who are poised to lead the Senate Finance Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee, respectively, in the upcoming Congress.
The lawmakers instructed the Trump administration to preserve all records pertaining to the tariffs and export licenses, as well as any communications with Nvidia and former CEO Jensen Huang, who announced his resignation on Thursday.
Wyden and Neal expressed alarm over reports that Trump and Lutnick were made aware of US intelligence indicating that Alice Huang—the Chinese businesswoman with whom Jensen Huang had an affair—was "funneling information to the Chinese government and facilitating Chinese access to advanced AI chips made by Nvidia." The New York Times reported that Trump "took no action" in response to the intelligence, which he was briefed on last fall.
During Trump's second White House term, Jensen Huang emerged as a leading ally of the president in the rapidly advancing artificial intelligence industry. Huang has been a frequent guest at Trump's White House and has donated tens of millions of dollars to the president's projects, including the ballroom.
Following news of Huang's resignation, Trump said the former Nvidia CEO "has done a fantastic job." The president had previously said Huang should remain the company's chief executive, calling him "an honorable guy."
Wyden and Neal wrote Thursday that "despite reportedly learning of Mr. Huang’s compromising relationship last fall, President Trump granted Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales." Lutnick, too, received classified information warning about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, according to Axios.
The lawmakers noted in their letter that Lutnick's Commerce Department halted an investigation into a Singaporean company suspected of smuggling Nvidia AI chips into China after an Nvidia executive intervened. The company under investigation was Megaspeed, where Alice Huang previously worked as managing director.
Facing subpoena threats, Huang agreed on Thursday to testify before House lawmakers in a closed-door hearing later this month, Bloomberg reported.

sources.news_title: Watch Trump Asked to Preserve Nvidia Documents by Senators
Preserve All Evidence: With Huang Out At Nvidia, Democrats Want Every Record Of His Calls With Trump
sources.text:
Preserve All Evidence: With Huang Out At Nvidia, Democrats Want Every Record Of His Calls With Trump
Hours before Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO on Thursday, two senior Senate Democrats told the Trump administration to preserve every record of its dealings with him, from his calls with President Trump to a Commerce Department probe of the chip buyer whose executive, a suspected Chinese spy, he has acknowledged a relationship with.
Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), the Banking Committee's ranking member, and Chris Coons (D-DE) sent the Nov. 11 letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller. It asks all three offices to keep every record on exports of Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China "or to entities that may divert such chips to China," to confirm in writing by Nov. 17 that preservation directives have gone out, and to brief members of Congress on the risks the suspected operation posed.
The list opens with the intelligence: every memorandum, assessment and briefing on the suspected operation involving Alice Huang, Jensen Huang or Megaspeed, including "the memorandum reportedly circulated to senior administration officials ahead of President Trump's visit to China in May 2026." The senators also want the "briefing materials, notes, and call transcripts" between Huang and Trump, and the records of Huang's meetings with senior officials on export controls, AI regulation and "proposed revenue-sharing or fee arrangements on chip sales."
Megaspeed, a Singapore-based computing company, has bought more than $4.8 billion of Nvidia's advanced AI chips since June 2024, according to the letter, and is reportedly under Justice Department investigation for diverting them to China. Commerce's own case against it was halted after Nvidia's general counsel reached out to the agents running it, as we reported. The letter asks for the August 2025 correspondence between that general counsel, Tim Teter, and Jeffrey Kessler, Commerce's under secretary for industry and security, Teter's reported call to Kessler about Singapore's detention of a Megaspeed executive, and every record on the probe's transfer, suspension or termination.
"This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government's ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security," Warren and Coons wrote. Officials at the White House, State and Commerce, they said, "were aware of concerns about NVIDIA, its relationship with Megaspeed, and the suspected Chinese intelligence operation, yet did not move to block the continued flow of advanced AI chips to Megaspeed."
The senators also asked whether "prudent defensive counter-intelligence action was taken or national security recommendations were overruled," and demanded the records on whether to give Nvidia's leadership a counterintelligence warning at all.
In a subsequent statement, Warren said that Huang's resignation "does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws." (we must have missed her letter about Dianne Feinsten's Chinese spy driver years ago)
Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA’s board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls. It’s clear that the American people cannot rely on Big Tech billionaire CEOs to put our national security above their bottom line – which is why Congress must pass the AI Overwatch Act and other bipartisan bills to keep advanced American AI technology out of China’s hands. Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China’s military. -Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA)
The request reaches back through every Trump-Xi meeting: the export-control talks ahead of the October 2025, May 2026 and September 2026 summits and the APEC meeting expected this month, Huang's seat on Trump's May 2025 Middle East trip, and Lutnick's invitation for Huang to meet Trump at Mar-a-Lago in April 2025. It also covers Nvidia's license applications under the Commerce Department's January 2026 rule on advanced computing chips, and the repeated suspensions of the rule extending export controls to affiliates of blacklisted companies.
Rubio briefed Trump on the intelligence about Huang aboard Air Force One in May, the New York Times reported, on the trip to China that Huang joined; the White House disputed the account. Trump said Monday that Huang told him, "I had no idea that she was a spy," adding, "And I really believe him." House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast (R-FL) said Tuesday he was prepared to subpoena Huang if he didn't answer by Wednesday the request from Mast and Reps. John Moolenaar (R-MI) and Rick Crawford (R-AR) for a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18, as we noted.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said on the Senate floor Tuesday that "Trump has been busy trying to defend Jensen Huang when he ought to be defending our national security," calling it "a dereliction of duty." Warren and Sen. Jim Banks (R-IN) on Sunday urged Congress to pass the AI Overwatch Act in the defense bill and told Commerce to close export-control loopholes.
Megaspeed, whose executive is at the center of the spy claims that Beijing has denied, said Thursday that it takes its obligation to comply with US export control laws "extremely seriously" and is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the U.S. government."
Huang resigned as president, CEO and director effective immediately on Thursday, a day after the Times reported a second affair, with an Nvidia vice president who reports to him. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, and Nvidia shares were down 11.9% in premarket trading, CNBC reported. The letter goes to the administration, not the company: its written confirmations are due Nov. 17, the day before the briefing House Republicans asked Huang to give.

sources.news_title: Nvidia preps exit strategy for Jensen Huang as Trump Administration is warned to preserve documents about its knowledge of spying and chip smuggling
sources.text:
Good morning. On Fortune’s radar today:
- Nvidia board plans exit for Jensen Huang.
- Huang’s affair with a subordinate was caught on video.
- We have a list of Huang’s possible replacements.
- Congress eyes probe of White House, chip exports, and Chinese spying.
- Markets: A divided house.
- AI’s $1 trillion annual cash transfer between buyers and suppliers.
- The “misery index” rises.
- This Cisco exec will walk out of meetings if staff use too many corporate acronyms.
ONE BIG THING
Nvidia preps exit strategy for Jensen Huang as Trump Administration is warned to preserve documents about its knowledge of spying and chip smuggling
Decisions are being made. It seems all but certain that Jensen Huang’s time as Nvidia CEO is coming to an end. Nvidia’s board met last night to discuss how to prepare for his removal. Since then, we have learned that they selected an outside firm to find candidates to replace him and that the board is considering naming a temporary CEO while the search goes on, according to Bloomberg.
Here are Huang’s possible replacements, per the FT:
- Finance chief Colette Kress.
- General counsel Tim Teter. He led much of Nvidia’s lobbying efforts in Washington, but that activity is now likely to come under congressional scrutiny (see below).
- Operations chief Debora Shoquist.
- Worldwide field operations chief Nick Parker, who joined the company last August.
- Chris Malachowsky, Huang’s engineer co-founder.
- Ian Buck, Nvidia’s data center business head, who has a deep background in the software that Nvidia’s chips use.
- ARM CEO Rene Haas. He previously spent seven years at Nvidia.
- AMD’s Lisa Su, Nvidia’s closest rival.
Huang’s fate was sealed when the NYT reported that he’d had a second affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care: “Mr. Huang, 63, and Ms. Powell, 48, were captured on video being affectionate at a San Jose, Calif., hotel during a Nvidia conference in March, according to two of the people who worked at the company. The New York Times has not seen the video.”
Alice Huang (no relation), Jensen’s other affair partner, has relocated to Beijing “with the knowledge of security officials,” according to Bloomberg. Alice is the founder of Megaspeed—which is currently under investigation by U.S. authorities for suspected chip smuggling—and a suspected Chinese spy.
A congressional investigation is now almost inevitable. Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons have asked the Trump administration to preserve all documents related to Nvidia, its exports, and Huang. That’s a common first step prior to a more formal inquiry.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is likely to come under scrutiny. After the Trump Administration restricted chip exports to China, Lutnick dragged his feet on enforcing the ban, to the bafflement of his cabinet colleagues, Axios reported.
And then there are Nvidia’s Singapore sales. The company used to report the top countries to which it sold products. As late as summer of 2025, 22% of the company’s business went to Singapore—an unusually large chunk given the small size of the city-state. But then Nvidia suddenly stopped reporting its country rankings, the WSJ said.
On Nov. 17, there is the small matter of Nvidia’s Q3 earnings call. Who will be the host?
- Nvidia preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang after affair with woman U.S. officials deemed a Chinese spy - Sebastian Herrera and Amanda Gerut
- How Megaspeed built a network in Singapore and Malaysia to move $7.5 billion of Nvidia chips to Chinese companies - Angelica Ang and Jay Ganglani
- Nvidia has lost $450 billion since Jensen Huang admitted to an affair. Millions of 401(k)s are exposed - Steven John
MORE FROM FORTUNE
The Layoff That Made People Want to Get Fired | Fortune Daily
Verizon’s CEO turned down the job several times before leaving retirement on his ranch: ‘I came in with a little bit of a bad attitude’ - Tatiana Sataua
Millennials wrote off accounting as the most boring job in America—now it’s one of the hottest seasonal jobs and Gen Z’s back door to six figures - Orianna Rosa Royle
Despite Trump Administration’s efforts to limit tariff refunds, American importers are one step closer to receiving $166 billion in universal rebates - Sasha Rogelberg
Jeff Bezos predicts AI could let families live on one paycheck. Amodei and Gates warn of a rougher road - Lara Murray-Sterzel
Mississippi elects first Democratic senator in 44 years as Dems finally find a winning strategy: Spend nothing and let the other candidate talk beef - Catherina Gioino
THE MARKETS
Nvidia fallout is splitting markets in two
Nvidia shares lost 5.54% overnight after the board convened to discuss replacing CEO Jensen Huang. Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at The Futurum Group, thinks the selloff is overcooked. The company’s “ecosystem [was] already firmly established long before this fiasco so I don’t see next 12 to 18 months of revenue suddenly disappearing if Jensen were to leave,” he told Fortune.
The Nasdaq Composite rose 1.6% yesterday, but Nasdaq 100 futures were down 0.67% before the open in New York this morning. Traders are picking between individual tech stocks and between tech and non-tech stocks. Nvidia is an obvious example. But yesterday, Oracle closed up 9%, and Tesla rose 3%, while SpaceX and Microsoft both fell 2.3%. Tech-heavy indexes in Japan and Korea both fell today, but markets in Europe, where industrials and finance carry more weight, were up.
- S&P 500 futures were down 0.29% this morning. The index rose 1.31% yesterday.
- In Europe, the Stoxx 600 rose 0.43% in early trading, and the U.K.’s FTSE 100 rose by 0.35% before lunch.
- Asia: South Korea’s KOSPI was down 0.61%. Japan’s Nikkei 225 was down 0.7%. India’s Nifty 50 was flat. China’s CSI 300 was down 0.78%.
- Brent crude declined to $92 per barrel.
- Bitcoin declined to $73,361.
Why CoreWeave’s stock popped: The AI neocloud is walking away from the corporate debt market
CoreWeave shares closed up 24.71% yesterday, following its Q3 earnings call. The company isn’t profitable, and as a debt-laden AI neocloud with massive outstanding commitments, you might be forgiven for asking why traders are suddenly so enthusiastic about a stock from which they previously axed 15%-plus of its market cap, year to date. Well, its revenue and adjusted operating income both beat expectations.
But the company also said it would begin eschewing the private credit market, according to Tim Hynes, Global Head of Credit Research at Debtwire, because the interest yields being demanded from companies issuing bonds to fund AI are now too expensive.
Debt on the balance sheet rose to about $47 billion from $35 billion in a single quarter, which seems like a lot, he said in an email.
But “the more telling message on the call was that management will not issue unsecured bonds at current yields through 2027,” he said. “In other words, the high-yield market has become too expensive for the company, and it is pivoting to customer prepayments … and to loans secured on chips and contracts.”
“The results buy time and credibility; they do not change the fact that this is a business that has to keep borrowing to grow."
WINNERS AND LOSERS
AI spending is essentially a $1 trillion annual cash transfer between buyers and suppliers
This elegant chart from Guillaume Jaisson at Goldman Sachs shows what appears to be a direct transfer of free cash flow from AI hyperscalers to the semiconductor makers they rely on. AI capex will reach around $800 billion in 2026 and $1.2 trillion in 2027, he estimates.
Even within the Magnificent Seven tech stocks, there are winners and losers when it comes to free cash flow, according to Tom Dalrymple at Aubrey Capital Management
“When a hyperscaler goes and buys chips from Nvidia, it capitalizes this cost and thus recognizes the expense over several years through depreciation, with most hyperscalers assigning useful lives of 5-7 years. This helps to dampen the impact on earnings from the investment,” he said in an email to Fortune. “Nvidia recognizes the revenue immediately upon delivery. This creates an earnings powerhouse, but the true cost shows up in the hyperscalers' free cash flow.”
So what?
“The same mechanism can just as easily reverse. Should capex stall, suppliers such as Nvidia would feel it immediately, while the hyperscalers would still be carrying years of depreciation on equipment already bought,” Dalrymple says.
CHARTS OF THE DAY
As the “misery index” rises, global central banks usher in a new era of expensive money
Central banks the world over have taken their gloves off when it comes to inflation, as this chart from James Pomeroy and Bethan Ellis at HSBC shows. “With the [Bank of England] raising rates in November, almost all of the hiking cycles we expect to see are now underway,” the pair said in a note.
One of the reasons the Fed and its foreign brethren are acting is because the “misery index” has started going up. The MI is the inflation rate plus the unemployment rate—which is on the rise in the U.S.
QUOTE OF THE DAY
“Until they put a face on the robot, and eyes, patients didn't want the device in their ward or in their room, but as soon as they added the face, they were much more accepting of it.”
—John Healy, vice president of the Industrial and Robotics Division of Intel, describing how robots made by Italy's Oversonic Robotics can become more effective at handling health care for the elderly. "What they didn't expect was that the patients respond far more willingly and openly to the robot than they did to the human practitioner," he told Fortune at Web Summit in Lisbon.
"When the robot asked questions about, you know, what the patient could remember or their recognition of the day of the week or anything that was sort of testing their current level of awareness, they had no shame responding to the robot. Whereas we believe that they may hold back in responding to the same questions to a human."
THE FRONT PAGES TODAY
Russian diesel exports double after Trump lifts sanctions, but US gets none - FT
Elon Musk says it would be an ‘honor’ to hire Nvidia’s Jensen Huang - CNBC
Outgoing Trump foe Massie forces new Epstein files showdown - Axios
United Airlines Is Banning AI Bots From Booking Flights - WSJ
US Envoys Arrive for Putin Talks as Zelenskyy Sees Opportunity - Bloomberg
In Major Upset, Scott Colom, a Democrat, Wins Mississippi Senate Seat - NYT
ONE MORE THING
This Cisco exec will terminate a meeting if you use baffling corporate acronyms
So you’ve heard of KPI, ROI, and EBITDA. But use the wrong acronym in front of this Cisco president and your meeting could be killed—especially if it’s one that nobody outside the building understands. “I don’t like acronyms, especially Cisco-manufactured acronyms,” Cisco’s president and chief product officer Jeetu Patel told Fortune at a small roundtable dinner.
“If there’s a meeting and there’s acronyms that are used, there are times that I’ve just terminated the meeting.”

sources.news_title: Democratic senators demand NVIDIA records from Trump administration over alleged Chinese spy ties
sources.text:
Democratic senators demand NVIDIA records from Trump administration over alleged Chinese spy ties
The letter to Rubio, Miller and Lutnick follows reports Jensen Huang had ties to a suspected Chinese intelligence operative
Two Democratic senators are demanding that the Trump administration preserve records related to Nvidia following reports that the company's CEO had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Chris Coons, D-Del., sent a letter Wednesday to Secretary of State and national security advisor Marco Rubio, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, calling on the administration to preserve documents, communications and other records related to Nvidia's exports of advanced AI chips to China and potential national security risks.
The request comes days after Nvidia's embattled CEO Jensen Huang acknowledged that he had been unfaithful to his wife in a relationship involving a woman described in reports as a suspected Chinese intelligence operative.
Huang's admission followed reports linking him to Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who has been described as an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.
NVIDIA PREPARING TO REPLACE CEO JENSEN HUANG AS SECOND ALLEGED AFFAIR EMERGES: REPORT
The letter adds to mounting scrutiny over the administration's handling of Nvidia chip exports and the allegations surrounding Huang, as Democratic lawmakers question what senior officials knew about the reported intelligence concerns and how they responded.
Warren and Coons said their inquiry followed reporting that senior Trump administration officials were aware of intelligence suggesting Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative, raising questions about whether appropriate national security precautions were taken.
"This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government's ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security," the senators wrote.
"Reports suggest that officials within the government – including at the White House, State Department, and Commerce Department – were aware of concerns about NVIDIA, its relationship with Megaspeed, and the suspected Chinese intelligence operation, yet did not move to block the continued flow of advanced AI chips to Megaspeed or other companies affiliated with the suspected operative," they continued.
NVIDIA STOCK FACES RARE DOWNGRADES AS BOARD INVESTIGATES CEO JENSEN HUANG'S ADMITTED AFFAIR
The senators also questioned whether "prudent defensive counter-intelligence action was taken or national security recommendations were overruled."
Megaspeed, the lawmakers noted, is a Singapore-based company that has reportedly purchased more than $4.8 billion in advanced Nvidia AI chips since June 2024.
The senators also cited reports that Megaspeed is under investigation by the Department of Justice for "potentially diverting advanced AI chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls."
They further pointed to reporting that a separate Commerce Department investigation involving the company was altered following communications with Nvidia representatives.
NVIDIA CASE HIGHLIGHTS RISKS OF ALLEGED 'HONEYPOT' SCHEMES TARGETING EXECUTIVES
The letter follows allegations from Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee that President Donald Trump dismissed a warning about Huang's reported ties to a suspected Chinese intelligence operative while his administration continued approving advanced chip exports to China.
In a post on X, committee Democrats alleged that Rubio warned Trump about Huang's relationship, "but Trump brushed it off."
"And instead of blocking sales of Nvidia's advanced chips to China, Rubio and Lutnick have continued to approve licenses for H200 chips to China," the lawmakers wrote.
Warren and Coons requested written confirmation by Nov. 17 that the administration had issued directives to preserve relevant records. They also requested a congressional briefing on the potential national security risks associated with the reported intelligence operation.
The senators specifically called for preserving communications between Nvidia executives and senior Trump administration officials, records related to investigations into potential smuggling of advanced AI chips, and decisions to weaken or suspend export controls on advanced AI technology.

sources.news_title: Senators fire opening shot at Trump aides over Nvidia CEO’s suspected spy affair: WSJ
sources.text:
Two incoming Senate committee chairs took aim at President Donald Trump's top aides over a scandal swirling around one of his tech allies.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) and Sen. Chris Coons (D-DE) are demanding that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller preserve every record tied to Nvidia's chip sales to China and CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday.
The senators gave the three officials until Tuesday to confirm they've told their staffs to hold onto all communications and other materials. Warren and Coons pointed to their incoming posts atop the Senate Banking and Foreign Relations committees, which oversee sensitive tech exports and national security.
The Journal noted that such letters tend to come before a formal congressional investigation. This letter arrives alongside a flood of similar demands aimed at companies and organizations closely tied to the administration.
The situation "raises significant concerns about the federal government's ability to effectively enforce our export controls," the pair wrote, adding that it also puts national security at risk.
They're seeking security and intelligence files on the suspected Chinese operation and Huang, any communications between Nvidia and the administration, including Huang's dealings with Trump himself, and records on chip export policy.
Huang forged a close bond with the president and personally pressed him to let Nvidia ship chips straight to China, all while carrying on an affair with Alice Huang, a former top executive at Singapore-based data-center firm Megaspeed International, The Journal reported. Nvidia's board was preparing to push him out over that affair and a second extramarital relationship, according to The Journal.
Warren and Coons have spent the past two years hammering Huang and the administration's decision to green-light chip shipments to China and other high-risk nations such as the United Arab Emirates.
The backlash isn't limited to Democrats. National Economic Council Director Larry Kudlow and Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-ND) had both urged Huang to resign by early Wednesday, while House Republicans, including Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast (R-FL), want Huang to brief lawmakers next week and have said they're open to subpoenaing him.
Rep. Michael Baumgartner (R-WA) went further, noting that Huang's signature motorcycle jacket has earned him a nickname in China and saying he hoped Congress wouldn't have to trade it for prison stripes over potential espionage or export control violations.
